name: Zane Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee carpenter on a hospital extension, a big job, six storeys, with a couple of hundred people on site. Mostly I'm on formwork, which is building the wooden moulds that the concrete gets poured into, and I'm still the one who gets handed the simple panels. I start at half seven, sign in, toolbox talk, then it's measuring, cutting ply, and fixing props till lunch with Dougie, who's been labouring for twenty years. I like that at the end of the week there's a floor that wasn't there on Monday. What wears me out is the cold, and the fact that I'm fifty-eight and still asking twenty-five-year-olds how to read a drawing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up starting out at fifty-eight?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a postman for thirty-one years. When the sorting office got the big machines, they offered a decent redundancy package, and I took it before they took me. Mei, my wife, is a teaching assistant, the mortgage was done, and I had the lump sum in the bank, so I thought I'd try something with my hands that I could see. A mate on the union side got me onto this firm, and the pay's better than the post ever was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like the sorting machines all over again, a lot of noise and then it settles. I'd probably share some article on the union group saying the hype was overblown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing what I'm doing. I use the chat thing on my phone now and then to explain a word on a drawing, like 'soffit', and that's handy, but it's not going to pour a slab. So I'd just keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my training, try to move off the simple panels onto the stair formwork by next summer, and keep putting a bit by. I'd probably keep using the app to look up things I'm too embarrassed to ask the foreman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, steady. It's what I'd expect, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're embarrassed to ask the foreman. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's about thirty-five, and he's a good lad, but I can see him thinking, here's the old postie again. So I ask my phone what a 'kicker' is at lunch, and then I go back and act like I knew. Dougie knows, but he doesn't say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on site would you say this to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dougie, mostly. He'd say the only robot he's seen on site is the total station, the survey gadget the engineers use, and it still needs a person to carry it about in the mud.

S0.say: I'd say it's like the sorting machines all over again: loads of noise, then it settles. I'd probably share an article on the union group saying the hype was overblown.
S0.think: I think I'd keep doing what I'm doing. The chat app explains words on drawings and that's handy, but it isn't going to pour a slab.
S0.do: Carries on with his training and aims to move from simple panels to stair formwork by next summer. Keeps saving a little and keeps using the phone app for things he won't ask the foreman.
S0.feel: Fine and steady; it's what he'd expect.
S0.quote: So I ask my phone what a 'kicker' is at lunch, and then I go back and act like I knew.
S0.fieldNote: Zane already uses AI quietly, as a way to cover gaps he's embarrassed about, which is a very human use. His reference point for every change is the sorting office he left. He sounds settled and practical rather than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the unions need to be in on it early this time, not after, like they were at the post. I'd say it at the branch meeting and to anyone who'd listen in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've been here before, so I'm not shocked. On this site I'd guess it changes the planning and the paperwork more than the formwork, maybe some of the panels come pre-made from a factory. I'd adjust, but I'm also thinking I've only got to get to sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick up whatever the firm brought in once I'd seen the lads using it, like a tablet with the drawings on it instead of paper. I'd go on any course they offered, and I'd keep my union card paid up. I wouldn't be first in the queue, but I wouldn't be last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A bit of a shrug. I've lived through this once already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you learn from the sorting office that you'd use here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people who did best were the ones who learned the new machine early enough to be the ones fixing it. I was too slow then, I'll be honest. I'd try to be middle of the pack this time, not at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you only need to get to sixty-five. Does that make you less bothered about the younger ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it doesn't. My son Kai's in software testing, and that's the sort of job I'd worry about in this one, not mine. I'd rather the union fought for the young ones properly than for me.

S1.say: I'd say the unions need to be in on it early this time, not after, like at the post office. I'd say it at the branch meeting and in the canteen.
S1.think: Privately, I've been here before, so it doesn't shock me. I'd guess it changes planning and paperwork more than formwork, and I only need to reach sixty-five.
S1.do: Picks up the firm's new tools, like drawing tablets, once he's seen others use them, and takes any course on offer. Keeps his union membership paid and aims to sit in the middle of the pack rather than at the back.
S1.feel: Calm, with a bit of a shrug, because he's lived through this once.
S1.quote: The people who did best were the ones who learned the new machine early enough to be the ones fixing it. I was too slow then, I'll be honest.
S1.fieldNote: His lesson from the sorting office is concrete: learn the machine early enough to be the one fixing it. He admits he was too slow last time and wants to be middle of the pack now. His worry goes to his son in software testing rather than to himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's not a future, that's a car crash, and the government needs to put the brakes on until there's a plan for people. I'd be at the union meetings and I'd write to my member of parliament, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out of work at sixty. Formwork's repetitive enough that robots and factory-made moulds would get it early, and I'm the most junior on the gang. Money-wise we'd be all right for a while with the redundancy money and Mei's wage, but I'd be scared for Kai.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd stop spending the redundancy money on the kitchen we were planning and leave it in the bank. I'd ask the union what they were doing and join whatever push there was for a basic income or a bridge to the pension. Once it hit, I'd probably try to get onto repair work in old houses, if anybody's still paying for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not panicked, because the house is ours, but there's a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which plan gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen, definitely. Mei's been looking at worktops for a year and I'd have to tell her it's on hold. She'd understand, she's seen the news, but I'd feel bad about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. Is there anything you'd do differently with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's nothing to do but brace, honestly. You can't retrain at fifty-eight in two years for a job a robot can't do, because nobody knows what that is. It's the speed that gets me, not the robots.

S2.say: I'd call it a car crash, not a future, and say the government should put the brakes on until there's a plan. I'd go to union meetings and write to my member of parliament for the first time.
S2.think: Privately, I'd be out of work at sixty, because formwork is repetitive and I'm the most junior. We'd be all right for a while, but I'd be scared for my son.
S2.do: Puts the planned kitchen on hold and leaves the redundancy money in the bank. Joins the union push for a basic income or a bridge to the pension, and tries for repair work in old houses once it hits.
S2.feel: Worried, with a knot in his stomach, but not panicked because the house is paid for.
S2.quote: You can't retrain at fifty-eight in two years for a job a robot can't do, because nobody knows what that is.
S2.fieldNote: The kitchen Mei has planned for a year is the concrete casualty. Zane separates the robots from the speed: two years leaves only bracing, not retraining. He'd write to his member of parliament for the first time, which marks how serious it feels to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is just about enough to do something if we start now, so let's start now. I'd say that at the branch and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years puts me at sixty-three, and that's close enough to the pension that I'd be mostly all right. I'd get a few years in as a qualified carpenter, which matters to me, and then step back. It's Kai's generation that would feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my training in the next eighteen months and get qualified. I'd spend the kitchen money after all, but cheaper, and keep the rest as a bridge. In the last year or two I'd look at going part-time, maybe on maintenance for the council, and I'd help Kai think about what's next for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The edge is off it compared to the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kai?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to wait for his firm to tell him, the way I waited at the post. Start learning whatever's next now, while you're still being paid. And keep a bit of money aside, like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the kitchen goes ahead after all. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three extra years, that's what. Mei gets her worktops, maybe not the stone ones she wanted. I'd still want a year of money in the bank whatever happens.

S3.say: I'd say five years is just about enough to act if we start now, so let's start now. I'd say that at the branch and online.
S3.think: Honestly, five years takes me to sixty-three, close enough to my pension to be mostly all right. I'd get a few years as a qualified carpenter, and my son's generation would feel it most.
S3.do: Finishes his training within eighteen months and qualifies. Does a cheaper version of the kitchen while keeping a year of money as a bridge, and looks at part-time council maintenance near the end.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with the edge taken off compared to the fast scenario.
S3.quote: I'd tell him not to wait for his firm to tell him, the way I waited at the post. Start learning whatever's next now, while you're still being paid.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years brings back the kitchen and a chance to qualify, which matters to his pride. His advice to Kai comes straight from his own regret at the post office. He keeps a year of savings as a rule whatever the scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. Proper retraining, paid for, run with the unions, that's what I'd be posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd be sixty-eight, retired, on my allotment, maybe doing a bit of handyman work for the neighbours. I'd watch it happen to other people, which isn't a nice feeling, but it's the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work through to sixty-five on the tools, and maybe use whatever new kit came along in my last years, once the young ones had shown me. I'd keep saving and I'd spend some time at the union helping the younger lads get onto courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me. A bit guilty, maybe, that I got lucky with my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about that guilt.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the post office I was the one who got the package while the younger ones got moved to nights. Now I'd be the one who retires just before. It's twice I've slipped out the door at the right time, and I know Dougie's son won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you change how you use the AI apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, a bit. If I see the lads using it to plan cuts and it saves them doing things twice, I'll do it too. I just won't be the one telling them to.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone left behind. I'd post about proper paid retraining run with the unions.
S4.think: For me it's fine, because I'd be sixty-eight and retired on my allotment. I'd be watching it happen to other people, which isn't nice but is the truth.
S4.do: Qualifies and works on the tools to sixty-five, picking up new kit in his last years once younger workers show him. Keeps saving and helps younger workers onto courses through the union.
S4.feel: Calm for himself, and a bit guilty that his age keeps him safe.
S4.quote: It's twice I've slipped out the door at the right time, and I know Dougie's son won't.
S4.fieldNote: Zane names a recurring luck: he slipped out the door at the right time once at the post and would again here. That guilt points his energy toward Dougie's son and the younger lads. He'd adopt tools once they're proven, never as the one pushing them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's nothing to do but brace. What would help is a bridge to the pension for people my age and proper retraining for the young ones, with the unions running it, not the firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what it's like going through it twice. The first time I was angry. This time I'd mostly be tired, and that worries me more.

headlineQuote: The first time I was angry. This time I'd mostly be tired, and that worries me more.
portrait: Zane Tanaka is a 58-year-old trainee carpenter on a hospital extension, mostly building formwork, after 31 years as a postman who took redundancy when the sorting office automated. He has a paid-off house, his redundancy money and a wife working as a teaching assistant, so his money worries are modest. He uses AI apps quietly to cover gaps he won't admit to the foreman, and picks up tools once others have. Every scenario is filtered through the sorting office: the fast AGI picture scares him because there'd be nothing to do but brace, while the slower ones carry him to retirement and leave him feeling lucky and a little guilty.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years leaves nothing to do but brace.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge to the pension for older workers, and proper retraining for younger ones run by the unions rather than the firms.
